source.title: Rethinking generative image pretraining: How far are we from scaling up next-pixel prediction?
source.authors: Xin-Chen Yan; Chen Liang; Li-Jun Yu; Adams Wei Yu; Yifeng Lu; Quoc V. Le

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. The paper text and metadata give different publication dates: the arXiv header says 17 May 2026, while the supplied year is 2025 and the paper states ICML 2026.
record.tranche_reason: It measures scaling of next-pixel prediction in image models, a new modality relative to the language-model claim, and reports scaling fits and downstream results.
record.gate_note: The study reports image-model scaling outcomes, so rows capture its own measurements and fits. It also cites language-model scaling results and discusses prior pixel-model results; those cited results are not recorded as rows. Projected results at 10^22–10^24 FLOPs are estimates, not measured runs.
record.test_reason: The study fits Hoffmann-style IsoFLOP power laws for raw-pixel autoregressive image Transformers (16×16 to 64×64; about 1e17–2.8e20 FLOPs). This is a new modality. It reports compute-optimal allocation exponents for loss and for two downstream metrics, and checks downstream predictions at 5× more compute.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add four points. The authors say pixel prediction follows predictable scaling trends like text, but needs 10–20× more tokens per parameter. Generation-optimal data must grow 3–5× faster than classification-optimal data. Higher resolution shifts the optimum toward model size. With compute growing 4–5× a year, they forecast feasibility within five years. They also caution that the 1e24 projections assume stable exponents over a 10,000× jump.
record.recipe_differences: Uses IsoFLOP profiles and power-law fits inspired by Hoffmann et al., adapted from language modeling to raw-pixel image pretraining and downstream image metrics. The study uses image tokens/pixels, not language tokens, and evaluates classification and conditional image completion as well as prediction loss.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported optimal parameter/data exponents vary by task and resolution. For 32×32, prediction loss, classification, and completion have different fitted exponents; the multi-resolution fits also shift toward faster parameter scaling at higher resolutions. The paper notes that the best-layer linear-probe results involve selecting layer and learning rate.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: Empirical scaling evidence is limited to image resolutions 16×16–64×64 and is reported up to 3.5×10^20 FLOPs for the stated extrapolation validation. The projections to 10^22–10^24 FLOPs are a 10,000× jump beyond the tested regime and assume stable exponents; the authors explicitly note possible qualitative shifts. Downstream evaluation is limited to ImageNet classification and image completion. The paper gives no error bars or confidence intervals in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result on the 10^22–10^24 FLOPs projected classification and completion outcomes was entered as an observed row because these are theoretical estimates, not measured runs (Tables 3–4). Qualitative completion samples and per-layer probing charts were not entered because they do not provide separate quantitative results for the claim versions recorded here (Figures 3, 8–14).

untested.parts: Not tested: the study trains no language models. Even for pixels, no loss-vs-compute power-law exponent or range is reported numerically.
Prediction is checked only at 5× compute. The 1e22–1e24 FLOP projections were never measured.
Not tested for language models, which are the version's target. Only the 32×32 pixel-loss allocation is fitted.
IsoFLOP variants perturb depth and width, but no fixed-parameter loss comparison across shapes is reported.
Not tested: video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes.
Not tested: whether downstream performance tracks pretraining loss. No loss-to-accuracy mapping is reported.

missing.what: Loss-optimal tokens-per-parameter ratio for pixels, over 400 vs about 20 for language (10–20× higher). This bears on how V3's Hoffmann allocation constants transfer across modalities.
Downstream accuracy and FD vs FLOPs across resolutions. Accuracy gains are only slight from 32×32 to 64×64 above 1e20 FLOPs, while FD keeps improving.

The authors' argument that Henighan et al.'s pixel scaling overestimated parameter scaling. They attribute this to using intermediate losses of longer runs (as in Kaplan), and report slower parameter scaling at 32×32 with IsoFLOP profiles.

record.verdict_notes: V3 is linked only from R1, because R2–R9 optimise downstream metrics rather than loss. The reader's V7 limits_scope label is replaced by supports, since V7 itself asserts that the split depends on setup. No uncertainty is reported on any fitted exponent. Fits use five IsoFLOP budgets per resolution, with 35 runs each.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures image models, not held-out pretraining loss of language models.
The paper tests a downstream prediction at 5× more compute, but does not test whether fits from small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.

Tests image-model optimal parameter and data allocation across compute for next-pixel loss, classification, and image completion; does not test language models or establish a universal allocation across all tasks and resolutions.
IsoFLOP variants perturb depth and width, but the study does not report a fixed-parameter comparison establishing that architecture details change loss only slightly.
Tests raw-pixel image pretraining at 16×16, 32×32, and 64×64 resolutions, and image classification/completion outcomes. It does not test video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes.

Tests ImageNet linear-probe accuracy and image-completion Fréchet Distance in image models; does not test language-model downstream tasks or a general relationship between downstream results and pretraining loss.

Shows task- and resolution-dependent fitted scaling exponents and optimal allocations. Does not experimentally vary fitting method, parameter-counting method, data, or training schedule to compare fitted laws, nor report curves bending away from a single power law.
